Department of Surgical Oncology, Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine Hangzhou China ([ROR:00ka6rp58](https://ror.org/00ka6rp58)) † Corresponding author ## Abstract Background:Approximately one-third of patients with HER2-positive breast cancer experienced recurrence within 10 years after receiving 1 year of adjuvant trastuzumab. The ExteNET study showed that 1 year of extended adjuvant neratinib after trastuzumab-based adjuvant therapy could reduce invasive disease-free survival (iDFS) events compared with placebo. This study investigated the efficacy and safety of pyrotinib, an irreversible pan-HER receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor, after trastuzumab-based adjuvant therapy in patients with high-risk, HER2-positive early or locally advanced breast cancer.Methods:This multicenter phase II trial was conducted at 23 centers in China. After enrollment, patients received 1 year of extended adjuvant pyrotinib (400 mg/day), which should be initiated within 6 months after the completion of 1-year adjuvant therapy (trastuzumab alone or plus pertuzumab). The primary endpoint was 2-year iDFS rate.Results:Between January 2019 and February 2022, 141 eligible women were enrolled and treated. As of October 10, 2022, the median follow-up was 24 (interquartile range, 18.0–34.0) months. The 2-year iDFS rate was 94.59% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 88.97–97.38) in all patients, 94.90% (95% CI: 86.97–98.06) in patients who completed 1-year treatment, 90.32% (95% CI: 72.93–96.77) in patients who completed only 6-month treatment, 96.74% (95% CI: 87.57–99.18) in the hormone receptor (HR)-positive subgroup, 92.77% (95% CI: 83.48–96.93) in the HR-negative subgroup, 96.88% (95% CI: 79.82–99.55) in the lymph node-negative subgroup, 93.85% (95% CI: 86.81–97.20) in the lymph node-positive subgroup, 97.30% (95% CI: 82.32–99.61) in patients with adjuvant trastuzumab plus pertuzumab, and 93.48% (95% CI: 86.06–97.02) in patients with adjuvant trastuzumab. The most common adverse events were diarrhea (79.4%), fatigue (36.9%), lymphocyte count decreased (36.9%), nausea (33.3%), and hand-foot syndrome (33.3%).Conclusions:Extended adjuvant pyrotinib administrated after trastuzumab-based adjuvant therapy showed promising efficacy in patients with high-risk HER2-positive breast cancer. The follow-up is ongoing to determine the long-term benefit.Funding:No external funding was received for this work.Clinical trial number:ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05880927 ## Introduction Worldwide, breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed malignancy in women. Approximately 15–20% of breast cancer cases are characterized by the overexpression of human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) (Siegel et al., 2014; Loibl and Gianni, 2017). Over the past 20 years, with the emergence of HER2-targeted agents, it has been proved that the addition of 1-year trastuzumab to adjuvant chemotherapy significantly reduces the recurrence rate and prolongs survival in patients with HER2-positive breast cancer (Perez et al., 2014; Cameron et al., 2017; Wolff et al., 2013). However, the phase III HERA study found that, despite receiving 1 year of adjuvant trastuzumab, 31% of patients with HER2-positive breast cancer experienced recurrence within 10 years (Cameron et al., 2017). In addition, the phase III APHINITY study reported a 12% recurrence rate in HER2-positive breast cancer patients with node-positive disease after receiving 1 year of adjuvant trastuzumab, pertuzumab, and chemotherapy with a median follow-up of 74 months (Piccart et al., 2021). Consequently, novel treatment approaches are warranted to extend the time to recurrence. Currently, the efficacy of extended adjuvant therapy has only been investigated in the phase III ExteNET study. The results showed that 1 year of neratinib after trastuzumab-based adjuvant therapy significantly improved invasive disease-free survival (iDFS) in women with HER2-positive breast cancer. However, the iDFS benefit did not translate into overall survival benefit in the intention-to-treat population after 8-year follow-up, except for patients with hormone receptor (HR)-positive disease (Holmes et al., 2023; Lüftner et al., 2021; Martin et al., 2017). Pyrotinib is an oral irreversible pan-HER receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), targeting epidermal growth factor receptor, HER2, and HER4 (Ma et al., 2019; Guan et al., 2023b; Xu et al., 2021). For patients with HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer, improved survival outcomes were shown in the pyrotinib group when compared with the control group in the phase III PHOEBE and PHILA studies (Ma et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2022). Additionally, results from the phase III PHEDRA trial demonstrated clinical benefits of pyrotinib plus trastuzumab and docetaxel for patients with HER2-positive early or locally advanced breast cancer in the neoadjuvant setting (Chan et al., 2016). In the present PERSIST study, our objective was to assess the efficacy and safety of administering extended adjuvant pyrotinib treatment following trastuzumab-based adjuvant therapy in patients with high-risk, HER2-positive early or locally advanced breast cancer. This report presents the efficacy and safety results with a median follow-up of 2 years, while longer follow-up is still ongoing. ## Methods ### Study design and participants This multicenter, single-arm, investigator-initiated, phase II exploratory study was conducted at 23 sites in China. The study protocol was approved by the institutional ethics committee of Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province and all other participating centers, and the trial was performed in accordance with the 2013 Declaration of Helsinki. This trial was registered at https://clinicaltrials.gov/ (NCT05880927). Written informed consent was obtained from all patients before study enrollment. Participants were eligible if they were women aged 18–75 years with high-risk, HER2-positive (immunohistochemistry 3+, or 2+ with gene amplification by fluorescence in situ hybridization) early or locally advanced invasive breast cancer; had previously completed 1 year of adjuvant therapy with either trastuzumab or trastuzumab plus pertuzumab within 6 months before enrollment; had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1; had known HR status; and had adequate bone marrow, hepatic, renal, and cardiac functions. High-risk patients were defined as those meeting one of the following criteria: N stage ≥1; T stage ≥2; absence of pathological complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant therapy; presence of pCR after neoadjuvant therapy but with tumor size ≥5 cm or N stage ≥2; tumor size <2 cm but with high Ki-67 level or histologic grade 3. Clinical and pathological stage was assessed according to the eighth edition of American Joint Committee on Cancer tumor-node-metastasis staging system. The expression of Ki-67 was categorized as low (<20%) and high (≥20%) based on the ratio of positive cells to all tumor cells in 10 high-power fields. The main exclusion criteria were bilateral breast cancer, inflammatory breast cancer, previous participation in other clinical trials involving anticancer therapy, allergies to the drug components in this protocol, history of immunodeficiency diseases, inability to swallow, and pregnancy or lactation. ### Procedure Pyrotinib 400 mg was administrated orally once daily within 6 months of completing trastuzumab-based adjuvant therapy. Concurrent adjuvant endocrine therapy for HR-positive disease was recommended. Treatment duration was 12 months unless intolerable adverse events, disease recurrence, death, or consent withdrawal occurred. ### Outcomes and assessment The primary endpoint was iDFS rate at 2 years. IDFS was defined as time from the initiation of pyrotinib treatment to invasive ipsilateral tumor recurrence, invasive contralateral breast cancer, local or regional invasive recurrence, distant recurrence, or death from any cause. The secondary endpoint was safety profile, graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.0. Patients were followed every 3 months for the first 2 years. The follow-up assessments included physical examination, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status, complete blood count, blood chemistry analysis, 12-lead electro-cardiogram, recording of adverse events, concomitant medications, and ultrasound. Computed tomography and bone scans may be conducted if clinically indicated. ### Statistical analysis Based on the previous ExteNET trial (Burstein et al., 2021), the 2-year iDFS rate was assumed as 91% in the present study. To restrain the width of 2-sided 95% confidence interval (CI) to no more than 0.1, 126 patients were required. Considering a dropout rate of 10%, a total of 140 participants were recruited. Continuous data were presented as median (range or interquartile range), while categorical data were presented as frequency (percentage). IDFS was estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, and the corresponding 95% CI was estimated using the Brookmeyer–Crowley method. Efficacy analysis was performed in the full analysis set, which included all patients who received at least one dose of study drug. Safety analysis was performed in the safety set, defined as all patients who received at least one dose of the study drug and underwent at least one safety assessment. ## Results ### Baseline characteristics Between January 2019 and February 2022, a total of 141 eligible women were enrolled in the study and received pyrotinib. All these patients were included in the full analysis set and safety set. The median age was 50 years (range, 25–72). Of the 141 patients, 107 (75.9%) patients had node-positive disease, and 64 (45.4%) had HR-positive disease. A total of 92 and 31 patients completed 1-year and 6-month treatment of extended adjuvant pyrotinib, respectively (Figure 1). ![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/101724/elife-101724-fig1-v1.jpg) #### Efficacy As of October 10, 2022, the median follow-up duration was 24 (interquartile range, 18.0–34.0) months. Of the 141 patients, seven patients experienced iDFS events, including one local recurrence, three brain metastases, two lung metastases, and one death due to distant metastasis. The 2-year iDFS rate was 94.59% (95% CI: 88.97–97.38; Figure 2). ![Figure 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/101724/elife-101724-fig2-v1.jpg) Subgroup analyses showed that the 2-year iDFS rate was 94.90% (95% CI: 86.97–98.06) in the 1-year treatment subgroup and 90.32% (95% CI: 72.93–96.77) in the 6-month treatment subgroup (Figure 3A). Concerning HR status, the 2-year iDFS rate was 96.74% (95% CI: 87.57–99.18) in patients with HR-positive breast cancer and 92.77% (95% CI: 83.48–96.93) in patients with HR-negative breast cancer (Figure 3B). In terms of lymph node status, the 2-year iDFS rate was 96.88% (95% CI: 79.82–99.55) in patients with lymph node-negative breast cancer and 93.85% (95% CI: 86.81–97.20) in patients with lymph node-positive breast cancer (Figure 3C). Regarding trastuzumab-based adjuvant regimen, the 2-year iDFS rate was 97.30% (95% CI: 82.32–99.61) in patients who received adjuvant trastuzumab plus pertuzumab, and 93.48% (95% CI: 86.06–97.02) in patients who received adjuvant trastuzumab (Figure 3D). ![Figure 3.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/101724/elife-101724-fig3-v1.jpg) **Figure 3.:** Kaplan–Meier curves for invasive disease-free survival in (A) patients who received 6-month (n = 31) and 1-year pyrotinib treatment (n = 92), (B) patients with hormone receptor-positive breast cancer (n = 64) and hormone receptor-negative breast cancer (n = 77), (C) patients with lymph node-positive breast cancer (n = 107) and patients with lymph node-negative breast cancer (n = 34), and (D) patients who received adjuvant therapy with trastuzumab (n = 92) and trastuzumab plus pertuzumab (n = 49). #### Safety The most frequently reported treatment-emergent adverse event was diarrhea (112 [79.4%]), followed by fatigue (52 [36.9%]), lymphocyte count decreased (52 [36.9%]), nausea (47 [33.3%]), and hand-foot syndrome (47 [33.3%]). Forty-three patients (30.5%) experienced grade 3 diarrhea, while no grade 4 or higher adverse events was reported (Table 2). Treatment discontinuation occurred in 11 (7.8%) patients, due to grade 3 diarrhea (n = 8), grade 3 hand-foot syndrome (n = 1), and intolerance (n = 2). ## Discussion To the best of our knowledge, this multicenter phase II study is the first prospective study to explore the efficacy and safety of extended adjuvant pyrotinib after trastuzumab-based adjuvant therapy in patients with high-risk HER2-positive breast cancer. Furthermore, while the ExteNET study only included patients who received neoadjuvant or adjuvant trastuzumab, over one-third of the patients in our study had received dual anti-HER2 blockade with trastuzumab and pertuzumab, making it more clinically applicable to current clinical practice (Bevers et al., 2023). In China, pertuzumab was approved for the treatment of HER2-positive breast cancer in the adjuvant setting in 2018, and has been covered by medical insurance since 2020. The PERSIST study started in 2019, thus the proportion of eligible patients who received trastuzumab and pertuzumab in our study was relatively high. In addition, we conducted subgroup analyses to explore the differences in the efficacy of extended adjuvant pyrotinib across different prior adjuvant regimens, including trastuzumab plus pertuzumab or trastuzumab alone, and different treatment durations. Currently, only neratinib has been approved by Food and Drug Administration in the extended adjuvant setting for patients with HER2-positive early or locally advanced breast cancer. In the 2023 National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines, it has been recommended for the treatment of high-risk, HR-positive, HER2-positive breast cancer (Nahta and O’Regan, 2012). In the ExteNET study, 1-year neratinib treatment after adjuvant trastuzumab significantly improved iDFS in patients with HER2-positive breast cancer, with a 2-year iDFS rate of 93.9% in the neratinib group and 91.6% in the placebo group (Martin et al., 2017; Burstein et al., 2021). In our study, the 2-year iDFS rate was 94.59%, comparable to that in the ExteNET study. In terms of subgroup analyses, the HR-positive group seemed to show a numerically higher 2-year iDFS rate than the HR-negative group (96.74% vs 92.77%). Consistently, similar results were observed in the ExteNET study. The underlying mechanism may involve cross-talk between HR and HER2 pathways (Pegram et al., 2023; Sudhan et al., 2019). Preclinical studies have shown that in estrogen receptor+/HER2+ cell lines, neratinib treatment also suppresses the activity of estrogen reporter (Hu et al., 2023). In the present study, adjuvant endocrine therapy was recommended for patients with HR-positive disease when treated with pyrotinib, which may generate synergistic effects (Zhang et al., 2022; Pivot et al., 2019). Regarding duration of treatment, the results showed that the 2-year iDFS rate was numerically higher with 1-year pyrotinib treatment (94.90%) versus 6-month pyrotinib treatment (90.32%). In the adjuvant setting, a phase III PHARE trial compared 1-year adjuvant trastuzumab with 6-month treatment, and the non-inferiority was not achieved for disease-free survival. Therefore, 1-year adjuvant trastuzumab remained the standard treatment (von Minckwitz et al., 2017). Further studies are warranted to find the optimal duration of extended adjuvant pyrotinib. Adjuvant treatment regimens before extended adjuvant treatment may also be associated with iDFS. In the present study, the 2-year iDFS rate was 93.48% and 97.30% in the trastuzumab subgroup and trastuzumab plus pertuzumab subgroup, respectively. The APHINITY study demonstrated a significantly improved iDFS with adjuvant trastuzumab plus pertuzumab than with adjuvant trastuzumab alone (von Minckwitz et al., 2019). Therefore, the iDFS benefits may last and affect the results in the extended adjuvant period. None of the patients in the PERSIST study received trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1), which is now a standard of care for HER2-positive patients with residual cancer after neoadjuvant therapy based on the phase III KATHERINE trial (Liang et al., 2024). Since T-DM1 was approved in China in 2020 and was not covered by medical insurance until 2023, it has not been widely used in clinical practice. Recently, a real-world study showed that patients with metastatic breast cancer could benefit from pyrotinib-based therapy after T-DM1 treatment (Shyam Sunder et al., 2023). Therefore, patients with high-risk breast cancer may also benefit from extended adjuvant pyrotinib after being treated with T-DM1 in the adjuvant setting, which needs further investigation. Regarding adverse events, diarrhea was the major safety concern in the present study, leading to treatment discontinuation in eight patients. This adverse event as well as vomiting and nausea are TKI-related common adverse events. The underlying mechanisms of these adverse events are not clear yet, and the mainstream hypothesis is that the growth and healing of epithelial cells in gastrointestinal tract are inhibited by TKIs (Secombe et al., 2020; Guan et al., 2023a). In the present study, 43 (30.5%) patients experienced grade 3 diarrhea, which were consistent with previous studies of pyrotinib (Guan et al., 2023b; Fang et al., 2022). Noteworthy, primary prophylaxis was not mandatory in this PERSIST trial. Currently, loperamide hydrochloride has been found to significantly alleviate symptoms of diarrhea and reduce diarrhea-related treatment discontinuation. It has been recommended for patients treated with pyrotinib (Zheng et al., 2023). In the PANDORA trial of pyrotinib plus docetaxel, the incidence of diarrhea was significantly lower in the loperamide prophylaxis group (8.9%) compared with the non-prophylaxis group (38.2%) (Barcenas et al., 2020). In the CONTROL trial, all cohorts that received loperamide prophylaxis and the dose escalation cohort of neratinib exhibited lower grade 3 diarrhea rates and fewer instances of diarrhea-related treatment discontinuation compared with ExteNET (Barcenas et al., 2020). The above two studies indicated that pyrotinib-related diarrhea could be controlled with prophylaxis or dose modification. There are several limitations in the present study. First, our study was a single-arm study without control group. Second, patients who received T-DM1 therapy in the adjuvant setting were not enrolled. Third, 27.0% of patients did not complete 1-year extended adjuvant pyrotinib due to COVID-19 pandemic or personal reasons. Finally, the follow-up time was short. A phase III clinical trial (NCT03980054) of extended adjuvant pyrotinib in patients with high-risk HER2-positive breast cancer is ongoing, which will further demonstrate the efficacy of extended adjuvant TKI and bring new hope for patients with high-risk HER2-positive breast cancer. ### Conclusions Our study suggests the potential of extended adjuvant pyrotinib in patients with high-risk HER2-positive early or locally advanced breast cancer after trastuzumab-based adjuvant therapy. The follow-up is ongoing to determine the long-term benefit of extended adjuvant pyrotinib. ### Clinical trial registration number This trial was registered at https://clinicaltrials.gov/ (NCT05880927).

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.101724.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.101724.3.sa1)

Summary:

This study introduces a novel therapeutic strategy for patients with high-risk HER2-positive breast cancer and demonstrates that the incorporation of pyrotinib into adjuvant trastuzumab therapy can improve invasive disease-free survival.

Strengths:

The study features robust logic and high-quality data. Data from 141 patients across 23 centers were analyzed, thereby effectively mitigating regional biases and endowing the research findings with high applicability.

Weaknesses:

(1) Introduction and Discussion: Update the literature regarding the efficacy of pyrotinib combined with trastuzumab in treating HER2-positive advanced breast cancer.

(2) Did all the data have a normal distribution? Expand the description of statistical analysis.

(3) The novelty and innovative potential of your manuscript compared to the published literature should be described in more detail in the abstract and discussion section.

(4) Figure legend should provide a bit more detail about what readers should focus on.

(5) P-values should be clarified for the analysis.

(6) The order (A, B, and C) in Figure 3 should be labeled in the upper left corner of the Figure.

Comments on revisions:

The authors responded well to my questions.

results.result: The PERSIST study enrolled 141 patients with high-risk HER2-positive breast cancer at 23 sites in China between January 2019 and February 2022, with patients receiving extended adjuvant pyrotinib (400 mg/day) for up to 1 year after completing trastuzumab-based adjuvant therapy. The median follow-up was 24 months, with 92 patients completing 1-year treatment and 49 discontinuing (11 due to adverse events, 38 due to COVID-19/personal reasons).
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C29, C66-C69, C74-C78, C82-C84 provide comprehensive study design, enrollment, and baseline characteristics that are internally consistent and clearly documented. The study methodology is well-defined with appropriate eligibility criteria, endpoints, and follow-up procedures.

results.result: The primary efficacy outcome showed a 2-year iDFS rate of 94.59% (95% CI: 88.97-97.38) in all 141 patients, with 7 patients experiencing iDFS events including local recurrence, brain metastases, lung metastases, and one death.
results.evaluation: Claims C13 and C30 are directly supported by the study data with appropriate statistical reporting including confidence intervals. The Kaplan-Meier curve (Figure 2) visually confirms the reported iDFS rate, and the specific breakdown of events provides transparency.

results.result: Subgroup analysis by treatment duration showed 2-year iDFS rates of 94.90% (95% CI: 86.97-98.06) in patients completing 1-year treatment versus 90.32% (95% CI: 72.93-96.77) in those completing only 6-month treatment.
results.evaluation: While the point estimates suggest better outcomes with longer treatment (C14, C15), the overlapping confidence intervals and small sample size in the 6-month group (n=31) limit definitive conclusions. The authors acknowledge this as a limitation (C61), and no statistical comparison between groups is provided.

results.result: HR-positive patients showed numerically higher 2-year iDFS rates (96.74%, 95% CI: 87.57-99.18) compared to HR-negative patients (92.77%, 95% CI: 83.48-96.93), potentially explained by cross-talk between HR and HER2 pathways and concurrent endocrine therapy.
results.evaluation: The observed difference in iDFS rates (C16, C17) is numerically present but lacks statistical testing for significance. The mechanistic explanation (C37, C38) is speculative and based on preclinical data with neratinib, not pyrotinib. The contribution of concurrent endocrine therapy (C73) as a confounder is acknowledged but not quantified.

results.result: Lymph node-negative patients had a 2-year iDFS rate of 96.88% (95% CI: 79.82-99.55) compared to 93.85% (95% CI: 86.81-97.20) in lymph node-positive patients.
results.evaluation: The reported rates (C18, C19) show overlapping confidence intervals, particularly the wide CI for node-negative patients (n=34), limiting interpretation. No statistical comparison is provided, and the small sample size in the node-negative group reduces precision.

results.result: Patients who received prior adjuvant trastuzumab plus pertuzumab showed a 2-year iDFS rate of 97.30% (95% CI: 82.32-99.61) versus 93.48% (95% CI: 86.06-97.02) for trastuzumab alone, with authors suggesting lasting benefits from dual HER2 blockade.
results.evaluation: While the numerical difference exists (C20, C21), the wide confidence intervals overlap substantially, and no statistical testing is provided. The interpretation that dual blockade benefits persist (C72) is speculative inference based on APHINITY results (C41) rather than demonstrated in this study. The unequal group sizes (49 vs 92) further complicate interpretation.

results.result: The most common adverse event was diarrhea (79.4%), with 30.5% experiencing grade 3 diarrhea leading to treatment discontinuation in 8 patients, though no grade 4 or higher adverse events occurred.
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C31-C34, C70 provide consistent and detailed safety data with specific frequencies and grades. The absence of grade 4+ events (C32) and clear documentation of discontinuations (C33) demonstrate adequate safety monitoring and transparent reporting.

results.result: The 2-year iDFS rate in PERSIST (94.59%) was comparable to the ExteNET study (93.9% for neratinib vs 91.6% for placebo), suggesting similar efficacy of extended adjuvant pyrotinib versus neratinib.
results.evaluation: The comparison (C36) is inappropriate as it lacks a control group in PERSIST. Comparing single-arm results to the treatment arm of a randomized trial (C35, C53) without accounting for patient selection, treatment differences, or temporal trends is methodologically flawed. The claim of "comparable" efficacy requires head-to-head comparison or proper indirect comparison methods.

results.result: The 30.5% incidence of grade 3 diarrhea was consistent with previous pyrotinib studies, and evidence from PANDORA and CONTROL trials suggests this could be controlled with loperamide prophylaxis, though primary prophylaxis was not mandatory in PERSIST.
results.evaluation: The consistency with prior studies (C63) is appropriately cited. The discussion of loperamide prophylaxis (C46-C49) is well-supported by external evidence, and the acknowledgment that prophylaxis was not mandatory (C60) provides important context for interpreting the high diarrhea rates.

results.result: The PHARE trial demonstrated that 6-month adjuvant trastuzumab was not non-inferior to 1-year treatment for disease-free survival, establishing 1-year trastuzumab as the standard treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C39 and C40 accurately represent established clinical trial results that provide context for treatment duration decisions. These are appropriately cited background claims supporting the rationale for 1-year extended adjuvant therapy.

results.result: T-DM1 is standard of care for HER2-positive patients with residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy, but was not used in PERSIST patients; authors speculate that extended adjuvant pyrotinib after T-DM1 may provide benefit based on real-world metastatic data.
results.evaluation: The standard of care status (C42) and Chinese approval timeline (C43) are factual. However, the speculation about benefit after T-DM1 (C71) extrapolates from metastatic disease data (C44) to the adjuvant setting without supporting evidence, representing hypothesis generation rather than demonstrated results.

results.result: The authors conclude this is the first prospective study of extended adjuvant pyrotinib after trastuzumab-based therapy, showing promising efficacy in high-risk HER2-positive breast cancer.
results.evaluation: The novelty claim (C54) appears reasonable but cannot be independently verified. The conclusions (C64, C65) of "promising efficacy" are limited by the single-arm design, short follow-up (median 24 months), high discontinuation rate (27%), and lack of control group. The term "promising" is appropriately cautious but the evidence base is preliminary.

results.result: Sample size calculation assumed a 2-year iDFS rate of 91% based on ExteNET, requiring 126 patients to achieve a 95% CI width ≤0.1, with 140 recruited accounting for 10% dropout.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 provide transparent statistical planning with appropriate justification. The actual enrollment of 141 patients (C11) closely matched the target, though the actual dropout rate (27%, C61) exceeded the planned 10%, which is appropriately acknowledged as a limitation.

results.result: Background context establishes that HER2-positive breast cancer represents 15-20% of cases, standard trastuzumab reduces recurrence but 31% still recur within 10 years, and extended adjuvant neratinib improved iDFS but not overall survival except in HR-positive patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6, C51-C52 accurately represent established epidemiological and clinical trial data with appropriate citations. These provide valid scientific context for the study rationale and are consistent with current knowledge in the field.

results.result: Pyrotinib is an irreversible pan-HER TKI targeting EGFR, HER2, and HER4, with demonstrated efficacy in phase III trials for metastatic (PHOEBE, PHILA) and neoadjuvant (PHEDRA) settings.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C9 accurately describe pyrotinib's mechanism and prior clinical evidence with appropriate citations. This provides valid rationale for investigating pyrotinib in the extended adjuvant setting.

results.result: Pertuzumab was approved in China in 2018 and covered by insurance since 2020; neratinib is the only FDA-approved extended adjuvant therapy and is recommended in NCCN guidelines for high-risk HR-positive HER2-positive breast cancer.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 provide factual regulatory and guideline information that contextualizes treatment availability and standards of care. These are verifiable facts that support the study's clinical relevance.

results.result: A phase III trial of extended adjuvant pyrotinib (NCT03980054) is ongoing, and 27% of PERSIST patients did not complete 1-year treatment due to COVID-19 or personal reasons, acknowledged as a study limitation.
results.evaluation: Claim C50 is verifiable through trial registries, and C61 transparently acknowledges a significant limitation affecting treatment completion. This demonstrates appropriate recognition of study weaknesses.

results.result: The mechanism of TKI-related gastrointestinal adverse events is hypothesized to involve inhibition of epithelial cell growth and healing in the gastrointestinal tract.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 appropriately presents this as a hypothesis ("mainstream hypothesis") rather than established fact, with supporting citations. The cautious language acknowledging uncertainty ("not clear yet") is scientifically appropriate.

results.result: The PERSIST study enrolled 141 patients with high-risk HER2-positive breast cancer across 23 centers in China who received extended adjuvant pyrotinib after trastuzumab-based therapy. With a median follow-up of 24 months, the primary endpoint showed a 2-year iDFS rate of 94.59% (95% CI: 88.97-97.38), with only 7 iDFS events occurring.
results.evaluation: Both reviewers explicitly accepted these core findings. The first reviewer stated 'the claims are fully supported by the types of experiments that were performed,' and the second reviewer praised the 'robust logic and high-quality data' from the multicenter design. No concerns were raised about the primary efficacy results or study conduct.

results.result: Subgroup analyses showed 2-year iDFS rates of 94.90% in patients completing 1-year treatment versus 90.32% for 6-month treatment, 96.74% in HR-positive versus 92.77% in HR-negative patients, 96.88% in node-negative versus 93.85% in node-positive patients, and 97.30% with trastuzumab plus pertuzumab versus 93.48% with trastuzumab alone.
results.evaluation: The reviewers did not question the subgroup analysis results. The first reviewer's statement that findings are 'fully supported' encompasses these analyses, and the second reviewer's request for better figure labeling (point 6) suggests acceptance of the data itself while seeking improved presentation.

results.result: The safety profile showed diarrhea as the most common adverse event (79.4%), with 30.5% experiencing grade 3 diarrhea. No grade 4 or higher adverse events occurred. Treatment discontinuation due to adverse events occurred in 11 patients (7.8%), primarily due to grade 3 diarrhea (n=8).
results.evaluation: Both reviewers accepted the safety findings without challenge. The first reviewer's endorsement that 'claims are fully supported' includes safety data, and the second reviewer noted 'high-quality data' without questioning the adverse event reporting or analysis.

results.result: The authors conclude that the 2-year iDFS rate of 94.59% in PERSIST is comparable to the ExteNET study (93.9% for neratinib vs 91.6% for placebo), demonstrating that extended adjuvant pyrotinib shows promising efficacy as the first prospective study of this approach in high-risk HER2-positive breast cancer.
results.evaluation: The reviewers accepted the comparative interpretation and novelty claim. The first reviewer stated the study 'provides fundamental findings and compelling evidence,' while the second reviewer acknowledged it 'introduces a novel therapeutic strategy' but requested more detailed description of novelty in the manuscript (weakness 3), indicating acceptance of the claim itself.

results.result: The authors propose that cross-talk between HR and HER2 pathways may explain higher iDFS rates in HR-positive patients, supported by preclinical data showing neratinib suppresses estrogen receptor activity. Concurrent endocrine therapy was recommended for HR-positive patients in the study.
results.evaluation: The reviewers did not challenge this mechanistic interpretation or the treatment protocol. The first reviewer's statement that findings are 'fully supported' and the second reviewer's focus on presentation issues rather than scientific interpretation suggest acceptance of this explanatory framework.

results.result: The authors discuss that pyrotinib-related diarrhea can be controlled with loperamide prophylaxis or dose modification, citing PANDORA and CONTROL trials. The 30.5% grade 3 diarrhea rate in PERSIST was consistent with previous pyrotinib studies, though primary prophylaxis was not mandatory in this trial.
results.evaluation: The reviewers accepted the safety discussion and comparison to prior studies. The second reviewer's request to 'update the literature regarding the efficacy of pyrotinib combined with trastuzumab' (weakness 1) suggests the need for more comprehensive literature review but does not challenge the diarrhea management claims presented.

results.result: The introduction establishes that 15-20% of breast cancers are HER2-positive, that approximately one-third experience recurrence despite adjuvant trastuzumab, and that pyrotinib is an oral pan-HER TKI with demonstrated efficacy in metastatic and neoadjuvant settings, providing rationale for the extended adjuvant study.
results.evaluation: The reviewers did not question the background literature or rationale. The second reviewer requested updating literature on pyrotinib combined with trastuzumab (weakness 1), indicating the background is acceptable but could be more comprehensive, not that it is incorrect.

results.result: The discussion contextualizes findings within the broader treatment landscape, noting that 1-year trastuzumab remains standard (PHARE trial), dual HER2 blockade improves outcomes (APHINITY), T-DM1 is standard for residual disease (KATHERINE), and over one-third of PERSIST patients received trastuzumab plus pertuzumab, which may have lasting benefits.
results.evaluation: The reviewers accepted this contextual discussion without challenge. The second reviewer's request for more detailed novelty description (weakness 3) and literature updates (weakness 1) suggests the discussion framework is sound but could be expanded, not that the comparisons are flawed.

results.result: The study methodology included specific definitions for high-risk patients, iDFS endpoints, safety assessments, follow-up schedules, and statistical assumptions based on ExteNET trial data. The authors acknowledge that 27.0% of patients did not complete 1-year treatment due to COVID-19 or personal reasons as a study limitation.
results.evaluation: The reviewers accepted the methodology but requested clarification. The second reviewer asked about data distribution and statistical analysis expansion (weakness 2) and requested p-values (weakness 5), indicating the methods are acceptable but presentation needs improvement, not that the approach is flawed.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect alignment on safety data (C22, C31-C34, C70). Both evaluations find the safety reporting well-supported with adequate documentation. OpenEval emphasizes transparent reporting of specific frequencies and grades, while peer reviewers accepted safety findings without challenge as part of 'high-quality data'.

Strong agreement on diarrhea management discussion (C46-C49, C60, C63). Both find the loperamide prophylaxis discussion and consistency with prior studies well-supported. OpenEval highlights appropriate external evidence citation, while peer reviewers accepted the safety discussion but requested more comprehensive literature review on pyrotinib combinations.

Strong agreement on core study design and baseline characteristics (C10-C12, C23-C29, C66-C69, C82). Both evaluations find these claims well-supported. OpenEval notes internal consistency and clear documentation, while peer reviewers praised 'robust logic and high-quality data' from the multicenter design. OpenEval covers additional claims (C74-C78, C82-C84) not explicitly mentioned in peer review.

Agreement on primary efficacy results (C13, C30). Both find the iDFS data supported. OpenEval emphasizes appropriate statistical reporting with confidence intervals and visual confirmation via Kaplan-Meier curves. Peer reviewers accepted these findings as 'fully supported' without concerns about primary efficacy results.

Agreement on background literature and epidemiological context (C1-C6, C51-C52). Both evaluations find these claims accurately represent established data with appropriate citations. OpenEval validates consistency with current knowledge, while peer reviewers accepted the background but suggested it could be more comprehensive.

Agreement on pyrotinib mechanism and prior evidence (C7-C9). Both find these claims appropriately cited and valid. OpenEval confirms accurate description of mechanism and clinical evidence, while peer reviewers accepted this rationale without challenge.

Significant disagreement on treatment duration subgroup analysis (C14, C15). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to overlapping confidence intervals, small sample size (n=31 in 6-month group), and lack of statistical comparison. Peer reviewers rated as SUPPORTED, accepting the subgroup analyses without questioning the limitations.

Disagreement on HR status subgroup analysis (C16, C17). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting the numerical difference lacks statistical testing and mechanistic explanation is speculative. Peer reviewers rated as SUPPORTED, accepting subgroup results without challenge. OpenEval also addresses mechanistic claims (C37, C38, C73) not evaluated separately by peer reviewers.

Disagreement on nodal status subgroup analysis (C18, C19). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to overlapping confidence intervals, wide CI for node-negative patients (n=34), and lack of statistical comparison. Peer reviewers rated as SUPPORTED, accepting the subgroup data without questioning precision limitations.

Disagreement on trastuzumab use subgroup analysis (C20, C21). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting overlapping confidence intervals, lack of statistical testing, and speculative interpretation about dual blockade benefits. Peer reviewers rated as SUPPORTED, accepting these subgroup findings. OpenEval also addresses related discussion claims (C41, C55, C72) about APHINITY extrapolation.

Major disagreement on comparative efficacy claims (C35, C36). OpenEval rates as UNSUPPORTED, identifying methodologically flawed comparison between single-arm PERSIST and randomized ExteNET treatment arm without proper controls. Peer reviewers rated as SUPPORTED, accepting the comparative interpretation and novelty claim without challenging the comparison methodology.

Disagreement on novelty and conclusion claims (C54, C64, C65). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting 'promising efficacy' is limited by single-arm design, short follow-up, high discontinuation rate, and lack of control group. Peer reviewers rated as SUPPORTED, accepting the novelty claim and acknowledging it 'introduces a novel therapeutic strategy' while requesting more detailed description.

Agreement on statistical planning (C79-C81). Both find the statistical methodology acceptable. OpenEval notes transparent planning with appropriate justification and acknowledges actual dropout exceeded planned rate. Peer reviewers accepted methodology but requested clarification on data distribution and statistical analysis expansion.

Agreement on background clinical trial context (C39, C40). Both evaluations find these established trial results appropriately cited. OpenEval confirms accurate representation supporting treatment duration rationale, while peer reviewers accepted this contextual discussion without challenge.

Partial agreement on regulatory context and speculation (C42-C44, C71). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, accepting factual regulatory claims but noting speculation about benefit after T-DM1 extrapolates from metastatic to adjuvant setting without evidence. Peer reviewers rated as SUPPORTED, accepting the discussion framework but requesting expansion.

Agreement on regulatory and guideline context (C56-C59). Both evaluations find these factual claims about regulatory status and standards of care well-supported. OpenEval confirms verifiable facts supporting clinical relevance, while peer reviewers accepted this contextual information without challenge.

Agreement on trial registration and limitation acknowledgment (C50, C61). Both find transparent acknowledgment of high discontinuation rate appropriate. OpenEval emphasizes recognition of study weaknesses, while peer reviewers accepted the limitation disclosure as part of acceptable methodology.

Agreement on mechanistic hypothesis (C62). Both evaluations find the cautious presentation of the 'mainstream hypothesis' appropriate. OpenEval notes proper acknowledgment of uncertainty, while peer reviewers accepted this discussion without challenge.

Disagreement on mechanistic interpretation (C37, C38, C73). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting the mechanistic explanation is speculative and based on neratinib preclinical data rather than pyrotinib, with unquantified confounding from endocrine therapy. Peer reviewers rated as SUPPORTED, accepting the mechanistic framework and treatment protocol without questioning the speculative nature.

Partial overlap on dual blockade discussion (C41, C55, C72). OpenEval rates interpretation as UNCERTAIN, noting speculation about persistent dual blockade benefits based on APHINITY rather than demonstrated in this study. Peer reviewers accepted the contextual discussion framework as SUPPORTED but requested expansion.
